title: Cost-based query plan selection
description: Cost-based planning estimates the work of candidate query plans and runs the cheapest, instead of trusting fixed rules. The planner enumerates join orders and access paths, costing each with table cardinalities and selectivities (cost = rows scanned + rows joined x factor); the minimum-cost plan wins. Good estimates routinely beat naive plans by orders of magnitude. Use it as the brain of any serious parallel query engine.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Predicate pushdown to storage
description: Predicate pushdown applies filters as close to the data as possible so the executor never moves rows that will be discarded. The planner rewrites the plan to push WHERE clauses into scan operators; a columnar scan then skips whole row-groups via min/max statistics without reading them. Less data moves, so parallel workers stay fed with useful work. Use it to cut I/O before parallelism even begins.
demo:
rows = [{"y": 2020}, {"y": 2024}, {"y": 2024}, {"y": 2019}]
pushed = [r for r in rows if r["y"] == 2024]
print("rows surviving pushed predicate:", len(pushed), "of", len(rows))
assert len(pushed) == 2
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Dynamic-programming join ordering
description: DP join ordering finds the cheapest order to join many tables by solving optimal subproblems bottom-up. The planner computes the best plan for every subset of tables (cost = best left + best right + join size estimate) and reuses them for larger subsets — classic Selinger-style optimization. It tames the factorial explosion of join orders. Use it for multi-way archive joins over catalogs, indexes, and metadata.
demo:
import itertools
sizes = {"a": 100, "b": 1000, "c": 10}
sel = 0.1  # join selectivity: result = left * right * sel
best, best_cost = None, float("inf")
for order in itertools.permutations(sizes):
    cost, cur = 0, sizes[order[0]]
    for t in order[1:]:
        cost += cur * sizes[t]; cur = cur * sizes[t] * sel
    if cost < best_cost: best, best_cost = order, cost
print("best join order:", best, "cost:", int(best_cost))
assert best == ("a", "c", "b")  # smallest-first greedy order wins

title: Fork-join recursive task splitting
description: Fork-join splits a query task recursively until pieces are small, solves them in parallel, then joins the partial results. A threshold decides when to stop splitting; worker threads steal or share the leaf tasks, and each join combines two partial results up the tree. It maps naturally onto divide-and-conquer queries like parallel aggregation. Use it for parallel sums, counts, and aggregations over archive partitions.
demo:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
def psum(xs, lo, hi, thr=1000):
    if hi - lo <= thr: return sum(xs[lo:hi])
    mid = (lo + hi)//2
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(2) as ex:
        l = ex.submit(psum, xs, lo, mid)
        r = psum(xs, mid, hi)
        return l.result() + r
data = list(range(10000))
print("parallel sum:", psum(data, 0, len(data)))
assert psum(data, 0, len(data)) == sum(data)

title: Thread-pool map over partitions
description: Thread-pool map applies a query function to every archive partition concurrently and gathers the results in order. Partitions are submitted to a fixed pool sized to the machine's cores; futures preserve submission order for deterministic output. It is the simplest correct way to parallelize embarrassingly parallel archive scans. Use it for per-partition filtering, scoring, and transformation.
demo:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
parts = [list(range(i*100, (i+1)*100)) for i in range(4)]
def hits(p): return sum(1 for x in p if x % 7 == 0)
with ThreadPoolExecutor(4) as ex:
    counts = list(ex.map(hits, parts))
print("hits per partition:", counts, "| total:", sum(counts))
assert sum(counts) == sum(1 for x in range(400) if x % 7 == 0)
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Scatter-gather query fan-out
description: Scatter-gather broadcasts one query to many archive shards and gathers their partial answers into a single response. The coordinator scatters the query with a deadline, collects shard responses as futures complete, and merges them (concatenate, then re-sort or re-aggregate). Slow shards are cut off at the deadline so one straggler cannot stall the answer. Use it for federated archive search across shards.
demo:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, wait, FIRST_COMPLETED
import time
def shard(n):
    time.sleep(0.01 * n); return [f"hit-{n}-{i}" for i in range(2)]
with ThreadPoolExecutor(3) as ex:
    futs = [ex.submit(shard, n) for n in range(3)]
    done, _ = wait(futs, timeout=5)
    merged = [h for f in done for h in f.result()]
print("gathered hits:", len(merged))
assert len(merged) == 6

title: Hash partitioning of archive data
description: Hash partitioning spreads archive records across workers by hashing the join or group key, so matching keys always meet on the same worker. Each record's key hashes modulo the worker count; joins and aggregations then run locally per partition with no cross-talk. Skew is the enemy — the executor monitors partition sizes and rebalances hot keys. Use it to parallelize joins and group-bys over archives.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Range partitioning for ordered scans
description: Range partitioning slices sorted archive keys into contiguous ranges so ordered scans and merges stay local. Split points divide the key space (by sampling or statistics); each worker owns one range, making range queries hit only relevant workers and merge steps trivially ordered. It suits time-ordered and ID-ordered archives. Use it for time-range archive queries and sorted merge joins.
demo:
keys = list(range(100))
bounds = [0, 25, 50, 75, 100]
parts = [[k for k in keys if bounds[i] <= k < bounds[i+1]] for i in range(4)]
print("range sizes:", [len(p) for p in parts])
q = [k for i, p in enumerate(parts) for k in p if 30 <= k < 60]
touched = [i for i, p in enumerate(parts) if any(30 <= k < 60 for k in p)]
print("range query touched partitions:", touched)
assert touched == [1, 2]

title: Partition pruning with min-max statistics
description: Partition pruning skips whole data partitions whose min-max statistics prove they cannot match the query predicate. Each partition stores min/max per column; a query like year=2024 skips partitions whose range excludes 2024 without reading them. It turns full scans into surgical reads. Use it to make large partitioned archives answer selective queries fast.
demo:
parts = [{"min": 2020, "max": 2021}, {"min": 2022, "max": 2024}, {"min": 2024, "max": 2026}]
def prune(pred):
    return [i for i, p in enumerate(parts) if p["min"] <= pred <= p["max"]]
print("partitions for year=2024:", prune(2024))
assert prune(2024) == [1, 2] and prune(2020) == [0]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Shuffle exchange for repartitioning
description: A shuffle exchange redistributes rows across workers by key between query stages, the fundamental data-movement operator of parallel engines. Each worker hashes its rows' keys and sends buckets to the owning workers; receivers merge incoming buckets into new local partitions. It is the expensive but universal glue between differently-partitioned stages. Use it between a filter stage and a join stage keyed differently.

t: Broadcast join for small dimension tables
title: Broadcast join for small dimension tables
description: A broadcast join copies the small table to every worker so the large fact table joins locally with zero shuffle. The planner broadcasts when the dimension table fits comfortably in memory; each worker hash-joins its local fact partition against the full copy. It avoids the most expensive operator in the plan. Use it for archive fact-to-dimension joins like records-to-categories.
demo:
dim = {"news": "News", "blog": "Blog"}
facts = [("news", 1), ("blog", 2), ("news", 3)]
joined = [(f, dim[c]) for c, f in facts]
print(joined)
assert joined[0] == (1, "News")
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Repartition operator for skewed keys
description: Repartitioning re-hashes data with salting on hot keys so skewed archive distributions still parallelize evenly. Hot keys get salted into sub-keys (key#0..key#N) for the heavy stage, then combined; the executor detects skew by partition-size sampling. This rescues group-bys dominated by a few giant keys. Use it when a few archive categories dwarf all others.
demo:
from collections import Counter
rows = ["news"]*90 + ["blog"]*10
salted = Counter(f"{r}#{i % 4}" for i, r in enumerate(rows))
print("max salted bucket:", max(salted.values()))
assert max(salted.values()) <= 30

title: Tree reduction for parallel aggregation
description: Tree reduction combines partial aggregates pairwise up a binary tree, finishing in logarithmic rounds instead of one serial pass. Workers aggregate their partitions, then pairs merge, then pairs of pairs, until one result remains; the combine operator must be associative. It keeps all cores busy right to the end of the aggregation. Use it for sums, counts, and max over huge archive scans.
demo:
parts = [10, 20, 30, 40]
level = parts[:]
while len(level) > 1:
    level = [level[i] + level[i+1] for i in range(0, len(level)-1, 2)] + ([level[-1]] if len(level) % 2 else [])
print("tree reduction ->", level[0])
assert level[0] == 100
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Parallel merge sort across workers
description: Parallel merge sort sorts each partition locally then k-way merges the sorted runs into one ordered result. Workers sort their chunks independently (even with different algorithms), then a tournament-tree merge repeatedly takes the smallest head. Total work stays O(n log n) with near-linear speedup. Use it for order-by queries over archives too big for one machine's memory.
demo:
import heapq
runs = [sorted([3, 1, 2]), sorted([6, 4, 5]), sorted([9, 7, 8])]
merged = list(heapq.merge(*runs))
print("merged:", merged)
assert merged == list(range(1, 10))
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Parallel prefix scan for running totals
title: Parallel prefix scan for running totals
description: Parallel prefix scan computes all running totals of an array in logarithmic depth using an up-sweep and down-sweep over a tree. The up-sweep builds partial sums bottom-up; the down-sweep pushes prefix values top-down, filling every position's running total. It parallelizes cumulative statistics like running document counts. Use it for cumulative archive metrics computed in parallel.
demo:
def prefix_scan(xs):
    # Blelloch up-sweep/down-sweep shape; final values filled sequentially here
    acc, res = 0, []
    for x in xs: acc += x; res.append(acc)
    return res
print(prefix_scan([1, 2, 3, 4]))
assert prefix_scan([1, 2, 3, 4]) == [1, 3, 6, 10]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice
